chapters.title: Chivalry On Stage
chapters.html:
“You’re kidding,” Mydei says drily, staring at the poster in despair.

Hyacine leans around him and squints. “‘The Grand Chrysos Competition,’” she reads, with a slight frown. “‘Join the contest and see who’s the—the most beautiful man in Tretos?’”

“The what?” Cipher asks, sounding delighted. She leans in over Mydei’s other shoulder. “Holy shit, you’re right. Wait, there’s more: ’Competitors will be judged on physical appearance, strength, chivalry, and’ —Oh my god, Phainon, you’ll love this one: ‘Fashion sense.’”

Mydei sighs through his nose. “We’ve lost already.”

Phainon crosses his arms. “Hey! I’m not that bad.”

“You’re wearing a crown,” Mydei tells him, as flatly as he can manage. “And you still don’t know how to tie your utility belts.”

Phainon makes an adjustment to his utility belts that he probably thinks is discreet. “I’m improving.”

He is not improving. He’s wearing the exact outfit that Mydei bought for him back when they escaped from the dungeons of Okhema City together. If he was responsible for dressing himself, Mydei is sure he’d still be in that goddamn yellow and purple ensemble. Phainon was utterly besotted with it. Mydei had to pull out all the stops—”Being conspicuous is a bad thing, Deliverer,”—to wrangle him into the white coat and blue cape he wears now.

“Well, it doesn’t matter,” says Hyacine brightly. “We can help you! I’m sure you’ll win. You’ve been on quite the journey to get here, after all.”

Cipher leans against the wall and gives them both a slanted grin. “You guys came all the way here for a beauty pageant?”

“We didn’t know it was—” Mydei sighs, looking at the ever-growing smirk on her face. Cipher just wants him to get mad again. With difficulty, he gives up. “Never mind. We can pivot. You’ll just have to learn chivalry and shit instead of stabbing your way to success like usual.”

“That’s much nicer to the other competitors,” Hyacine says brightly, patting Phainon’s shoulder. “And it doesn’t get your sword dirty! Isn’t that great?”

“Huh,” says Phainon, his eyes wide. He fumbles at his belt for his cleaning cloth.

“For the last fucking time,” Mydei says, exasperated. “It’s clean. You haven’t even fought anything since the last time you wiped it down. You don’t need to clean it. I could lick your sword and I’d only taste cleaning chemicals.”

“I suppose we’ve no choice,” Phainon says eventually, lifting his gaze towards the sun-stained sky. “Well then! Tretos’ Grand Chrysos Competition, here we come.” Then he steps through the city gates with all the confidence of a true prophesied Deliverer.

Hyacine follows, then Cipher. Mydei brings up the rear and follows Cipher closely enough to glare at her a little. She snickers under her breath.

“What?” Mydei hisses to her, quiet enough to avoid being overheard.

Cipher side eyes him with a shit-eating grin. “You’d love to lick his sword, wouldn’t ya?”

“Shut the fuck up.” He kicks her for good measure. She’s too fast, of course, and dodges the hit easily. It just makes her laugh at him harder.

It’s kind of pathetic, his crush on Phainon. It’s been there in the back of his mind for months, practically since he and Phainon first broke out of prison together. It’s that damn Deliverer’s attitude of his. He’s a hero, and he knows it. Mydei had thought, before all this, that he’d never fall victim to a hero’s legendary charms, and yet here he is. Still traveling with Phainon after all this time.

He should probably suck it up and leave. Phainon has Hyacine and Cipher to look out for him now—it’s not like he’s going to get mauled by wild boars at their camp at night. He doesn’t need Mydei, not the way he did when they first started out. But alas. Here he is. Stuck with Phainon and his dumb crush on him until the end of eternity.

And now Cipher knows. Great.

“You’re really obvious,” Cipher says conversationally, turning around to fully face him while walking backwards.

“Watch the road, Cipher.”

She ignores him, as usual. “Honestly, I’m surprised he hasn’t called you out on it yet. One of these days he’s gonna look at you from across the campfire and go, Hey Mydei, why do you always look at me like you want me to kiss you stupid?”

“I do not,” Mydei says, appalled. His mind helpfully supplies an image of Phainon leaning in so eagerly that they both topple over with the force and fall on their asses in the dirt. It’s weirdly endearing.

“Ah, sorry,” Cipher says. “I forgot you’re already stupid.”

Mydei kicks her again. Cipher cackles and actually backflips over his kick like the obnoxious show-off she is.

“Cipher? Mydei?”

Both of them immediately fall back in line at the sound of Hyacine’s voice. “Yes ma’am,” Cipher says, practically sprinting to catch up to her. Hyacine watches with a little smile on her face.

Hyacine is standing in front of a red-roofed house with linen curtains. Mydei wipes the sweat off his forehead with one hand and glances around. Their hero is nowhere to be seen.

“Phainon went inside,” Hyacine says, before he can even ask. “This is where the competition organizer lives. He’s negotiating for the Coreflame.”

Ah, fuck. Mydei immediately bolts for the door, but when he reaches for the doorknob, he finds something restraining his hands. He glances down. It’s Hyacine’s threads of water magic. Mydei turns around to her, disbelieving. “You’re leaving him alone in there?” he hisses. “He’s a country boy. This is a fucking mafia town. They’ll eat him alive.”

“You,” Cipher points out, “would kill them without thinking twice.”

“I might think once at least.”

“Yeah. You’d think, Let’s kill these guys, and then you’d do it.”

Mydei doesn’t want to admit that she’s probably right, so he leans against the wall of the house. His breath sits in the humid, hot air around him like a cloud of ill will. The air is unpleasantly soupy. He’s used to dry heat, not… whatever this is. The sweat clings to him with a vengeance. Their party has been on the road for a week. The only thing he’d been looking forward to was the fighting competition. And now they find out there’s not even a battle at the end of this arduous journey. Just his luck.

“Well, at least it can’t get much worse,” Mydei mutters, dragging himself up from the wall to stand again.

And then the door slams open, and Phainon comes tumbling through it.

Cipher and Hyacine both catch him before he can hit the ground. He wheezes and takes both their hands to stumble to his feet. Then he scrubs a hand over his face.

“Not good, I take it?” Hyacine asks, already scanning him with magic for injuries.

“Never,” Phainon wheezes, “let me negotiate again.”

Hyacine smiles sympathetically and heals the scrape on his back. He looks unharmed, aside from getting a bit banged up when they threw him out. That’s better than nothing, at least.

“We still need the Coreflame,” Mydei says, pacing back and forth. “If they won’t negotiate, then we’ll need to find another way. There’s always theft, but these guys are serious. Cipher could do it, but she’d need my help to distract them. Still, it’s risky… You think we could switch it out during the contest? Bribe someone? Negotiate with the winner?”

Phainon frowns. “What happened to competing?” he says, pouting a little. “The Coreflame is the prize; all we have to do is win first place, and we get it fair and square.”

Right. Mydei forgot that he’s weird like that. He always wants to win things honestly. “Hate to break it to you, but I don’t think you’re winning any chivalry contests.”

The thing about Phainon is that his bad ideas strike out of thin air. He’ll be totally fine and logical one moment, and then all of a sudden he’ll come up with the worst idea known to man. And then he’ll get his heart set on it, and he won’t give up until he’s seen it through. The problem is, once Phainon has a bad idea—

“But we’ve got the most handsome man in all of Amphoreus right here,” Phainon says. Then he looks directly at Mydei for a solid second. Two. Three.

Mydei stares at him, baffled. “What?”

“Trust me,” Phainon says. He shoots Mydei his signature smile, that sun-blinding grin. “What could go wrong?”

—Once he has a bad idea, nothing can change his mind.

***

Tretos isn’t a big city. Originally, it was just a poorly disguised mafia hideout masquerading as a harbor town, but now there are some law-abiding residents who just like the atmosphere. Mydei can’t imagine why—the weather is pitifully bad. By the time they arrive at the town’s single inn, it’s almost nightfall, and yet the air is still sweltering and damp.

Phainon moves to stride through the inn door with confidence. Before he can enter, Cipher zips in front of him and blocks his way. “What happened to never letting you negotiate again?” she asks, grinning at him.

Phainon’s face is a little flushed when Mydei finally catches up. He smiles sheepishly. “Sorry. Here.” He hands Cipher his wallet. “You go in.”

“Not the whole thing,” Mydei says, snatching it back from her. “Just give her enough for the usual rooms.” He separates out the appropriate amount of credits, plus a little extra just in case, and gives Phainon his wallet back.

“Ya got me,” Cipher sighs, but takes the offered money with a cheerful wink.

Once she’s vanished into the inn, Phainon turns on him with a slight frown. “She isn’t going to steal from us, Mydei. You don’t need to be so cautious.”

Mydei crosses his arms. He leans against the inn wall, trying to stay in the sliver of shade it affords him. He closes his eyes. “You don’t know how criminals work. Don’t give her the temptation.”

“Just because she was a thief before joining us doesn’t mean she’s still one now.”

“People don’t change, Deliverer.”

A hand on his shoulder. A sigh next to his ear. Mydei doesn’t dare open his eyes; he knows Phainon is right next to him. Probably too close. If he opens his eyes now, it’ll spell disaster.

“But you’ve changed,” Phainon says softly, his voice lower than usual. “Look at yourself, Mydei. From the dungeons of Okhema to the Deliverer’s most trusted companion. My most trusted companion. My—”

“Shut up,” Mydei mutters, shoving vaguely at the space over his shoulder. Only when he feels his hand connect does he open his eyes. Phainon looks hurt, downcast. He’s so readable. Guilt wells up in Mydei’s chest. He opens his mouth to apologize, but no words come out.

Phainon drops his eyes to the cobblestone sidewalk. “No, you’re right. I shouldn’t say that.”

“Deliverer,” Mydei says, reaching out for his shoulder. “Phainon. I’m not angry at you. It’s just—”

“FUCK YOU TOO THEN, YOU LITTLE SON OF A—”

It’s Cipher’s voice, at top volume. Hyacine’s eyebrows shoot into her hair. She hurries into the lobby of the inn. Before Mydei can find the words, Phainon has followed her inside.

Mydei watches them go and doesn’t follow. He stands there in the meager shade of the balconies overhead and wallows in his misery. He never knows what to say to Phainon. He’s sweaty again. His hair is damp against his neck. Fuck this town.

“Mydei?” Hyacine asks, leaning her head out of the doorway.

Mydei startles at her voice. He forgot they’d be expecting him. “Just let me know when you’ve got the rooms.”

“Well, that’s the problem,” she says delicately. “Their rooms are booked up with competitors for the festival. The only room they have available is on the… ah, the second floor.”

“So?”

Hyacine’s smile is a little pinched. “It’s the women-only floor. With dedicated guards.”

Ah. Mydei sighs. He gets the necessity—he’s met a lot of women traveling alone over the years, and they’d probably be grateful to have their own floor. He can’t even complain about it, not when he’s seen women more likely to sleep on the road than at an inn with a bar downstairs. “You and Cipher can stay here, then. Phainon and I will be fine. We’ve slept on the road before.”

“That’s the thing,” Hyacine says carefully. “Phainon is being very…”

“—Please? I’m begging you. If there is anything at all available, we’ll take it. I don’t care where it is, or what’s going on with it, but we just—”

“…Insistent.”

“Obstinate,” Mydei fills in for her. He sighs and scrubs a hand over his face. It doesn’t help. His hands are just as sweaty as the rest of him. “I’ll talk to him.”

Hyacine gives him a watery smile. She taps his shoulder, and healing magic rushes through him. It isn’t necessary, and it’s dumb of her to use her magic when he doesn’t really need it, but the gesture is nice. It makes him stand a little straighter, at least.

“Phainon,” he calls as he enters the inn. “Stop being—”

“Just the man I was looking for,” Phainon interrupts loudly. His smile is strained. “As I was saying, this is Miss Cipher’s husband. Can they not stay together?”

Mydei nearly walks right back out.

“Ah, well, that might be doable,” the innkeeper says hastily, shooting Cipher a faintly terrified glance. “We could arrange for him to stay in the spouse’s section of the women’s floor, just outside the guards…”

“Great,” Phainon says, his smile flashing his sharp teeth. He slams his wallet down on the counter. “Give me the keys.”

The innkeeper looks at him, confused. “But, sir, you’re not…”

“He’s with me,” Mydei says, crossing his arms. If it makes his muscles look a little more intimidating, that’s only a convenient side effect. “Give him the keys.”

The innkeeper gives Phainon the keys.

Hyacine gives a friendly little wave as the four of them file into the inn. It only makes the innkeeper look more terrified. Well, Mydei supposes the damage is done.

As soon as they’re in the stairwell, Cipher bursts into giggles. “My husband? You know I’m gonna marry for money, right? This bastard is broke as shit.”

“It was the only thing I could think of,” Phainon says, ducking his head with a small smile. “Sorry, Cipher.”

Cipher gets an apology, but not him? Mydei bites down a scowl. He manages to hold his tongue until Cipher and Hyacine say goodbye to them on the second floor.

The guards don’t let them past the barrier, but they let Mydei into the first room down the hall with his spouse pass. He unlocks the door and kicks off his shoes. It’s a small room, one bed and a little desk and a chair. He does have a private bathroom, though, complete with a bathtub and running sink.

“It’s not terrible,” Phainon says, putting his hands on his hips with a little exhale. “Maybe my negotiating skills are alright.”

It is a good room for the price they paid. Mydei can’t bring himself to feel happy about it. “What about you?” he asks, a little sharper than he intends. “The three of us all have a place to sleep, but you’re on your own.”

Phainon’s mouth flattens out a little. “Don’t worry about it. I’ll find somewhere.”

“You’ll find somewhere.” Mydei narrows his eyes. “Quit bullshitting me.”

“I’ll take a guard shift. They’ll let me sleep at the desk.”

“They’re already suspicious,” Mydei points out. “That won’t work.”

“Then I’ll… go up to the higher floors! I’ll just ask around. Bring some credits.”

“And let every competitor in the festival see you groveling?”

Phainon frowns slightly. “Stop being so contrary.”

“I’m being realistic,” Mydei snaps. Then he exhales harshly and wipes the dampness from his face yet again. “It’s too damn hot here.”

Phainon looks him right in the eyes. “Then take off your clothes.”

His eyes are crystal clear in the evening light from the window. Mydei’s throat goes dry. He locks eyes with Phainon and fumbles with the hem of his shirt. Phainon holds eye contact and moves closer, one slow step at a time, until his hands are on top of Mydei’s and he’s pulling the shirt over his head.

Mydei throws the shirt onto the bed. Then, slowly, he reaches for his belt.

Phainon’s hand lands on top of his, stopping him in his tracks. “Close the window.”

Mydei rolls his eyes, but yanks the curtains closed regardless. His heart is racing. It’s terrible—each heartbeat makes him hotter, like his blood is simmering underneath his skin. Then, with one of Phainon’s hands still on his hip, he undoes his belt and takes his pants and underwear off in one go.

Phainon makes a half-laugh through his nose. “No striptease?” he asks, grinning with his teeth.

“I’m being efficient,” Mydei replies, his voice strangled. “I just need to cool down.”

“Uh huh,” Phainon says. He starts unwrapping the bandages on Mydei’s arm, carefully winding them around his hand to save the fabric. Underneath is the nastiest scar Mydei’s ever received: a long gash, a souvenir from the murder that landed him in Okhema’s dungeons. A souvenir from his father. But Phainon never seems to mind the ugly, half-healed flesh, so Mydei lets him undo the fabric covering and stands, nude, across from him.

Once the bandages are fully undone, Mydei has nothing left. It’s just him, and a fully-clothed Phainon, standing in the inn room they aren’t supposed to be sharing.

“You didn’t need to say that,” Mydei says eventually, looking at the rolled-up bandages on Phainon’s hand instead of at him. Like a coward. “You could have gotten the room for yourself. I’ve been on my own before.”

“And I haven’t?” Phainon asks pointedly.

“You know that’s not what I meant.”

“I won’t know what you mean unless you tell me.”

“You’re the Deliverer.” He hates the way it sounds when he says it: like a royal title, like a punishment, like a curse. “Deliverers don’t have to fend for themselves. Deliverers have people to rely on.”

“I do. I rely on all of you.”

“Then take the damn room. Stop being ridiculous. The bed is fine. The bathroom is nice. And you can clean your sword all you like without me around to complain.”

Phainon laughs weakly. “Can’t I just like to keep my belongings clean?”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then tell me,” says Phainon firmly, “what the point is.”

Mydei looks at him. At his sparkling eyes and his unshakeable hero’s devotion. His stupid heart does something weird in his chest. “Why me?” he asks quietly. “Phainon, why would you choose me over yourself?”

Phainon’s expression softens. “That’s all?” he asks, smiling a little, like he’s in on some joke Mydei doesn’t get yet. “That’s what you’ve been worried about?”

Rather than say yes, or lie, Mydei crosses his arms.

“You’ve been suffering out here,” Phainon says gently. “Don’t lie to me—I can tell you’re more tired than usual. You just said it; it’s too hot for you. And besides, we need you in your best condition for winning the Grand Chrysos Competition. Gotta earn that Coreflame prize, right?”

Mydei nearly laughs with relief. “Idiot,” he says, a little breathless. “You’re still trying to win the competition? Cipher and I can just steal it.”

“But you’re so handsome,” Phainon says, pouting. He runs one hand across Mydei’s collarbones, then down his chest, over the war paint patterned onto his skin. “The minute they see you, the competition will be over. You won’t have to even lift a finger.”

Mydei huffs another half-laugh. “I’m filthy. Get your hands off me.”

“Mm. Aren’t you glad I got you the room now?” Phainon asks, grinning. “You can take a bath.”

Mydei can’t even argue with that point. A bath sounds heavenly right now. He’s so fucking sweaty and gross and the water will feel so good. And then he’ll get to sleep in a bed for the first time in a week.

“Fine,” Mydei grumbles. He drags himself into the bathroom and begins drawing a bath. The tub is slow to fill, but the water heats up quickly. He stands by the faucet, watching the water level gradually rise. Phainon follows him inside and stands right behind him. He sets his chin on Mydei’s shoulder, so his mouth is right next to his ear.

“Let me help you,” he says, already reaching out to undo Mydei’s braid.

At his sides, Mydei’s fingers twitch. Undoing braids is personal. Intimate. He doesn’t think Phainon knows, but still, it’s not something he needs help with, exactly. “You want to wash my hair?” he asks, skeptical. “Why?”

“Because you’re competing for us all. And your hair is prettier when it’s freshly washed.”

Mydei can’t object to that. Phainon’s helped wash his hair before, but always at campsites or on the road. Places where it’s difficult to do it alone. Never at an inn, where Mydei is more than capable of doing it himself.

“And because,” Phainon murmurs, running his hand down the side of Mydei’s throat, “I like to keep my belongings clean.”

“Your—” Mydei splutters. His heartbeat roars in his ears. “Your what?”

“My belongings.” Phainon slowly gathers his hair in both hands and lets it fall down his back. “That which belongs to me.”

Mydei feels lightheaded. “I am not your sword, Deliverer.”

Phainon just laughs breathily by his ear. His hands are still settled on Mydei’s collarbones, fingers tracing idle patterns on his skin. “Yet you fight at my command all the same. Isn’t it only right that I should want to keep you spotless?”

Mydei takes a long, measured inhale and wills the heat away from his face. “I actually hate you,” he mutters, and then he gets into the bath and turns off the tap, leaving his hair facing towards Phainon. Silently, he hands him the shampoo.

Phainon’s breath is steady and amused behind him. “You wouldn’t have broken me out of prison if you hated me.”

It’s a good argument, and not one he can refute. He’d already been working on an escape plan from the Okheman dungeons when Phainon got thrown down there. They put Phainon in the highest security cell, reserved for the worst criminals in the city-state. Mydei never asked why. He just threw a blue cloak at him and told him to come along. They’ve been together ever since.

If only Mydei hadn’t been dumb enough to rescue a hero. Damn Deliverer, making him a hero alongside him. He should have just stayed in prison.

“I hate this town,” Mydei says aloud, as Phainon begins rinsing his hair.

Phainon sighs. “I don’t like it, either. But we need all twelve Coreflames, and they’ve got one.”

Mydei doesn’t need to be told the importance of the Deliverer’s mission. He’s known it ever since he first met Phainon, since he saw the determination in his steps. “It weighs on you,” he says softly, turning his head back. “Doesn’t it?”

Phainon smiles wryly. “I can’t wash your hair at this angle.”

Mydei keeps looking at him. Phainon looks back. His eyes gradually soften, the usual shield of enthusiasm melting away. There’s an odd sorrow behind his eyes, the type of sorrow that can’t ever be drowned.

“Stay here,” Mydei says, apropos of nothing. “Just—share the bed with me. They won’t come in. They won’t care.”

“They might be suspicious,” Phainon argues, though it sounds half-hearted. “You’re supposed to be a married man and all.”

“Forget about that.”

Phainon presses his fingertips into Mydei’s temples, gently massaging the headache away. It feels heavenly. When Phainon tilts his head back into position, he obeys easily. Phainon washes his hair in silence. When he rinses the shampoo out of Mydei’s hair, he hums an unfamiliar tune to himself, so quietly that his voice breaks on some of the notes.

His hair is filthy enough that Phainon goes back for a second round of shampoo, this time holding up the top of his hair to work at the underside. His hands are careful as he separates out the layers of Mydei’s hair.

“Hold this,” he says quietly, and guides one of Mydei’s hands up to hold the top layer of his hair.

Mydei takes it. He catches a glimpse of Phainon’s reflection in the water’s surface, with his coat and his crown and his worn eyes. “Phainon,” he says. “Did you want to be a Deliverer?”

Phainon exhales a long, slow breath. “Did you want to be a murderer?” he asks, barely above a whisper.

Mydei doesn’t know how to answer that. His eyes are heavy. He tips his head back and lets Phainon continue his work in silence.

***

“No.”

“But it’s so pretty!” Hyacine looks up at him with big, round eyes. “Please, Mydei? You won’t have to do anything. I’ll lace it up myself. All you have to do is stand there.”

“We are not spending two hundred thousand credits on a corset,” Mydei says firmly. “Let alone a corset that I’ll wear one time for a competition, and never again.”

Cipher lowers the corset so that her face peeks over the top. “What I’m hearing is that we need to find opportunities for you to wear it all the time.”

Mydei groans. He turns to Phainon, arms crossed over his chest. “Talk some sense into them.”

“I mean,” says Phainon, looking at him through the corner of his eye.

“Deliverer.”

“It looks good!” Phainon protests, throwing up his hands in defeat. “Sue me for wanting to see you in it, okay?”

Mydei stares at the corset. It’s red with pink lacing up the back, only boned in the front. It doesn’t look terribly uncomfortable, as far as corsets go, and its ties are flexible enough that even he, with his straight-line waist and bony hips, might fit into it. He hates it all the more for its plausibility. He sighs and brushes the corset away. “I would sooner compete shirtless.”

“Great!” says Phainon, beaming as he reshelves the corset. “Okay, that’s half the budget saved. Let’s go.”

Mydei raises his eyebrows. “What?”

“You just said you’ll compete shirtless. So we can move on. Do you think a skirt or pants is more chivalrous?”

Hyacine hums, furrowing her brow. “It’s very warm here. Perhaps a skirt would be more appropriate?”

“And don’t forget better shoes,” Cipher says, kicking at his feet. “These aren’t sexy at all.”

“Ow,” Mydei hisses, glaring at her. Then, “Wait. I never said that.”

Cipher raises her eyebrows. “Yeah you did. Just now.”

Mydei gapes at her. Instead of the corset? “I didn’t mean—”

Phainon looks at him with his stupid faith-filled eyes glimmering wet and says, all innocence, “You didn’t?”

This little bastard. Who let him become a hero? Mydei shoves him away and rolls his eyes. “Quit it already. If you think I should do it, I’ll do it.”

“You totally should!” Hyacine says, beaming. She’s given up on the corset remarkably fast. Suspicious. Mydei is starting to wonder if this was their goal from the beginning. “You’ve got a great build. Showing it off is a surefire way to increase our chances of winning.”

“If you’ve got it, flaunt it,” Cipher says, shrugging. “Hate to say it, but you’ve really got it, man.”

Mydei’s face feels warm. He ducks his face and walks away from the clothing shop. “I already said I’ll do it. No need for flattery.”

Phainon grins and skips up alongside him. “But you deserve it. Don’t you like hearing how beautiful you are?”

If he wasn’t red-faced before, he definitely is now. He huffs an exhale. “Weren’t you trying to find the most chivalrous skirt to put me in?”

Phainon looks at him sideways, his mouth slanted with amusement. “You want me to dress you?”

Point taken. Mydei follows Hyacine to the next stall.

The town is set up with dozens of pop-up clothing stands for the festival. Evidently, many people come here for the competition without adequate chivalrous clothing. Either that, or they start to doubt their wardrobe and decide to expand it. The main street is packed with competitors and attendants and vendors, all fighting for attention. Cipher can dart through the crowd like it’s second nature, but Mydei never quite learned the art of light-footedness, so it takes him a while to find his way over.

By the time he reaches the next stall, Hyacine is already holding up something with a gleeful smile on her face.

Mydei has a bad feeling about this. But when he examines it, nothing seems amiss. It’s a long red skirt with elegant draping and a metal belt at the waist. “Oh,” he says, a little surprised. “It’s actually nice.”

Hyacine lights up like a beacon. “You like it?”

Mydei takes the hanger from her. He swishes the skirt through the air, watching it move. The fabric is gorgeous, shimmering blood-red in the sunlight. “I’ll try it on.”

Hyacine beams. “He said yes!”

“Ooh, great,” Cipher says, appearing out of nowhere from underfoot, and snatches the skirt back from him without further ado.

Phainon finally appears at the stall, looking winded. He leans one hand against the stall frame. Between gasps, he asks, “How do you guys—get through the crowd—so fast?”

“Skill issue,” says Cipher, reappearing again. “Anyway, we bought the skirt. All we need now are some sexy thigh boots. Maybe a giant necklace to make people look at your tits.”

Mydei stares at her. “Some what?”

“Sexy thigh boots. And a necklace.”

Mydei can’t even muster up the energy to be surprised. He just sighs. “You know what? Yeah. Get me sexy thigh boots. I don’t even care.”

Cipher looks elated. She grabs Hyacine’s hand and rushes off, vanishing back into the crowd.

“Seriously?” Phainon asks, still winded. “I just got here.”

Mydei can’t even see their heads anymore. “Whatever. Let them go.” He drags them off the main street, down an alley leading to the water.

Tretos is a port city, but the water isn’t particularly picturesque and the port is shallow, so it’s still relatively uncrowded by the docks. He takes Phainon to the shadiest spot he can find and plunks himself onto the ground, sighing in relief.

Phainon sits down next to him with a groan. He tips his head back against the wall. The heat must be getting to him, too. Mydei wisely switched to shorts today, and the lightest shirt he owns, so the climate is slightly more bearable. Phainon, on the other hand, is still wearing his armor and his dumb crown and everything.

“It’s so fucking hot here,” Mydei mutters, throwing his head forward to put his hair up.

Without being asked, Phainon gathers all his hair in one hand and holds it for him while he wraps the ribbon around it.

“Thanks,” Mydei says quietly.

“Don’t mention it.”

They sit there watching the murky water and the floating moored boats. Their meager sliver of shade grows slimmer by the second as the sun climbs higher.

“We’re really doing this?” Mydei asks eventually, looking up at the cruel sky. “The competition?”

Phainon wheezes out a laugh. “Well, you are.”

“I thought you were supposed to be the chivalrous one, Deliverer.”

Phainon tips his head back too, so they’re looking at the same spot in the cloudless sky above them. “It’s like you said. Deliverers have people to rely on.” He looks over at Mydei, just briefly. “You’re one of them.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “Sappy.”

“No one ever claimed I wasn’t.”

Mydei glances at him. “You’re really okay with it?” he asks, a last-ditch effort. “With people—looking at me? At my body?”

“Why wouldn’t I be?” Phainon asks, sharper than usual. “It’s your decision, not mine.”

Mydei’s eyes are still burning with the afterecho of the bright sky. He can’t see Phainon’s expression clearly. He’d been half-hoping for jealousy. But they aren’t like that. They’ve never really been like that. Phainon is the Deliverer; Mydei is an escaped murderer. And besides, he isn’t special. Everyone’s in love with the dashing knight in shining armor. “Yeah,” he says, closing his eyes. “Yeah.”

***

Hyacine and Cipher evidently hadn’t stopped at the shoes. As Mydei unpacks the bag back in their room, he just keeps finding more accessories: bracelets, cuffs, rings, even a hair cuff. With difficulty, he wrangles himself into the skirt and the belt, and the secondary belt they bought, and the boots, which are beautiful black leather and woven iron, and are indeed thigh-high. Then he turns back to Phainon.

“So?” he asks. “Thoughts?”

Phainon holds out the necklace. “You forgot something.”

It’s an enormous gold and silver masterpiece, made of two different pieces chained together to form one piece of statement jewelry. Phainon is slow as he fastens it, letting his hands drag against Mydei’s collarbones. He turns Mydei to face him, leaving his hands on his shoulders longer than necessary.

Phainon makes a show of looking him up and down, his eyes lingering and slow. “It’s good,” he says eventually. “Try moving around?”

Feeling a little ridiculous, Mydei walks a straight line across the room and back again. The necklace clinks gently as he moves, and the tall boots move with his legs easily. It’s surprisingly convenient. These might even enter his regular repertoire of clothing.

“The skirt is a little narrow,” Mydei says eventually. It’s the only flaw he can find. “I can’t take full-length steps in it.”

Phainon frowns at the skirt like he can shame it into compliance.

“In Kremnos,” Mydei says, his heartbeat loud in his ears, “we cut slits into them for easier movement.” Then, before he can think better of it, he reaches out and takes Phainon’s sword from his belt.

Phainon visibly swallows. He places his hand atop Mydei’s on the sword. “Let me do it.”

This is a terrible idea. This is the worst idea he’s had in years. And yet he guides Phainon’s sword out of its sheath and presses him down slowly, bringing Phainon to his knees and the sword to the bottom hem of the skirt.

Phainon takes in an unsteady, audible breath. He looks up at Mydei with wide eyes. “You want me to—while you’re wearing it?”

Mydei nods. Then, with all the courage he has, he says, “I trust you.”

Slowly, deliberately, Phainon drags his sword up the fabric. The skirt slices easily under the touch of his sword, parting like he was always meant to claim the space between its threads as his own. He stops just above Mydei’s knee, his blade hesitating.

Mydei grabs his hand before he can retreat. “Higher.”

Phainon pulls the blade up another six inches.

“Higher.”

Three inches.

Surely his range of motion is fine by now, with a slit this long. “Higher,” Mydei demands anyway, because he can’t help himself.

Phainon doesn’t move. “Mydei,” he says weakly, looking up at him again. “Mydei, really, I mean—you want me to—”

“Do it, Deliverer,” Mydei breathes.

Phainon slices the skirt all the way up his thigh. The cold press of the blade against his bare leg sends chills down his spine. It’s the flat side, not the sharpened edge; the touch doesn’t hurt, but it feels almost electric with anticipation. His heart is singing in his chest as Phainon draws his sword away.

“My bad,” Phainon says, running his hand up Mydei’s thigh underneath the slit. His hand pauses at the top, then drags over the fabric to settle on his hip. “I might have cut it a little too high.”

Mydei’s head is spinning. “If I asked you to cut it higher, would you?”

“Have mercy, Mydei,” Phainon says weakly. He stands up to his full height again, then steps back, examining the outfit. “Walk again? I want to see it in motion.”

Mydei walks the length of the room again. He takes wider steps, as long as he comfortably can. He can feel air swishing against his leg, nearly up to his hip. Phainon doesn’t once look him in the eyes as he walks. It’s immensely gratifying, holding his attention like that.

“We need to balance it,” Phainon blurts, seemingly out of nowhere. “With the side slit, you need something on the other side to even out the visual weight.”

Mydei glances down. Usually he’d take the opposite of whatever Phainon’s fashion advice is, but he’s right this time. He could use something on his left side, perhaps higher up, to balance out the look. “I’ll just wear the fabric bandages like usual.”

“I think,” says Phainon quietly, “you should wear this instead.”

And he takes the silver pauldron off his shoulder.

Mydei’s mouth goes dry. He stands there, completely still, as Phainon adjusts the leather straps to fit around his chest. When he finally pulls back, with the armor secured, he looks Mydei up and down one last time. “There. Now you look the part.”

Mydei looks down at himself. Phainon’s silver Deliverer’s armor glints at him from the corner of his eye. “I look like something of yours.”

The silver and gold of the necklace glints in Phainon’s eyes. “Yes,” he says, leaning in a little closer. “Exactly.”

***

Tretos’ Grand Chrysos Competition has nearly five hundred competitors. They’re all numbered off in order of registration, one through four hundred and ninety-one. Mydei is number four hundred and five. He lines up in his spot and lets Hyacine fuss over every accessory on his outfit with her brows furrowed and tries not to sweat to death.

“Do you think four rings, or three?” Hyacine asks, holding up his left hand. “Oh, and which fingers? And do you want to braid the rest of your hair? Not that it looks bad—it looks great—you look great—do you want a drink? Did you have enough breakfast?”

“For fuck’s sake,” Mydei mutters.

Hyacine shoots him a reproachful look.

“No, thank you,” Mydei hastily corrects himself. “I ate plenty. Three rings would look better.”

“Stop worrying so much,” Cipher groans, propping her chin on Hyacine’s shoulder. “If our resident man candy doesn’t win the contest, all we gotta do is steal the Coreflame. Easy peasy.”

“It’d be easier not to steal things at all,” Hyacine says, in that holier-than-thou tone. But then again, Mydei supposes she is a priestess. That’s pretty damn holy.

“Phainon doesn’t like theft,” Mydei agrees, shrugging his shoulders to even out the pauldron’s weight. Phainon didn’t fasten it quite right; he still hasn’t learned how all those straps work. “But we don’t have to tell him about it.”

Cipher punches his uncovered shoulder lightly. “You got this, you little bastard. And if you don’t, it’s whatever. Nine lives, right?”

Mydei breathes out, softens his shoulders. He nods.

“Mydei!”

Ah. Great. The hero himself. Mydei looks at him, exasperated already. “What now?”

Phainon skids to a stop in front of him. He looks smaller without his pauldron. His hair is mussed with sweat. “I brought you this,” he says, and holds out a tiny fruit tart like a sacrificial offering.

Mydei blinks. “A fruit tart?”

“I spent all morning asking around for the best bakery,” he says proudly. “And this one was the winner. I bought three, by the way. One for now, and two for after you win.”

Mydei takes the fruit tart, oddly touched. “Stupid use of your time,” he says halfheartedly. He takes a bite of the tart.

Oh. Wow.

Before Mydei has realized it, he’s shoved the whole thing into his mouth. The tart is full of blueberries and sliced figs and grapes, and even some pomegranate kernels. The crust is flaky and crisp, and the custard underneath is smooth, and the glaze on top is sweet. It might be the best fruit tart he’s ever had.

“Good?” Phainon asks, looking up at him with those dumb hopeful eyes.

Mydei wipes the crumbs off his mouth with the back of his hand. “Didn’t get much fruit in prison.”

“So that’s a yes.”

Mydei sighs. “Yes, Deliverer. It was good. Now leave me alone—it’s almost my turn to compete.”

“Okay, okay,” Phainon says, holding up his hands. He turns around. Cipher and Hyacine follow suit, heading out to the viewing area to watch his competitors, where they’re on number three hundred ninety-nine.

Mydei turns to watch the stage. He isn’t quite nervous, exactly, but he’s not confident, either. He shifts the pauldron straps again.

“Wait, Mydei—”

Phainon is standing next to him again.

Mydei huffs. “What do you want? They’re about to call me.”

“Just…” Phainon hesitates. Something flickers across his expression briefly, then vanishes just as quickly. “Good luck, Mydei.”

He reaches out and touches Mydei’s braid. Mydei holds his breath as he runs his fingers along it.

“It was untucked,” Phainon explains, too late to be believable.

Mydei knows damn well it wasn’t. Hyacine fixed it only minutes ago. “Thanks,” he says anyway.

Phainon looks at him. He opens his mouth. His breath ghosts across Mydei’s nose.

“Good luck,” he repeats. Then, with great difficulty, “Mydei, I—well, I—what I’m trying to say is, you should know that I—”

“Four hundred and four!”

“I’m next,” Mydei reminds him. “You should get to the audience.”

Phainon’s expression crumples. He takes a deep breath. “Alright. I’ll see you after the contest, then.”

And then Mydei is being whisked up to the stage, having his directions repeated to him for the dozenth time, and he’s nodding along, and then the announcer calls his number and he’s on the stage, with thousands of eyes trained on him.

Mydei walks to center stage with all the confidence he can muster. At the mark on the floor, he pivots dramatically to face the audience. Then, he takes his stance.

The contest is a performance at heart. Most serious contestants have rehearsed their programs for weeks. Mydei, however, has had a grand total of three days to prepare. So he defaults to the one thing he knows best: the fight.

He and Phainon have dueled a thousand times. Sometimes as practice; sometimes to settle disputes; sometimes as a form of apology. They duel so often that it’s become a familiar rhythm. A punch thrown, a punch dodged. A kick thrown, a kick dodged. A headlock, an escape. A tackle, a flip. So Mydei gets on stage and challenges the imaginary Phainon in his mind, and then they fight.

Stage fighting is tough, especially on his own. There’s no Phainon on stage to actually knock him back. He has to capture himself in the headlock, and escape from it all on his own. It’s not a long fight, but it is an intense one. Mydei has rehearsed it on his own, just a few times, each one different from the last. Every time, he shaped the fight so that he won. But this fight—this imaginary challenge against the Phainon in his mind—is different.

And as the clock runs out, Mydei realizes that he’s accidentally structured this fight so that he loses.

When his performance time is up, Mydei swallows his pride and yields to the imaginary opponent he’s been fighting. Then, with his head held high, he bows to his nonexistent opponent—and to the watching crowd—like a real knight would. Like a graceful loser, ready to take second place with a smile.

The crowd goes wild.

Phainon pounces on him the minute he exits the backstage area. “Mydei!” he cries, like they haven’t seen each other in years. “Mydei, that was amazing. I could see the fight happening from both sides, even with just you. It was beautiful. Why don’t you do that more? I want to watch.”

“You watch me lose plenty,” Mydei tells him, wiping his face with the towel Hyacine hands him. “I lose to you all the time.”

“But not like that,” Phainon insists. “Not like—like you’ve been waiting your whole life to lose that fight. Like it’s an honor.”

Mydei’s face is warm. He scrubs at his face harder with the towel. If only Phainon knew that he was imagining that defeat at his hands. His pathetic, heroic, forever-clean, sword-worn hands. “You’re reading too much into it.”

“He’s right, though,” Cipher says, slapping his back. Mydei jumps—he didn’t know she was behind him. “Those other guys ain’t shit. You nailed that.”

“Don’t insult the other competitors,” Hyacine reprimands gently. “They all tried their best. If their best wasn’t as good as Mydei’s, that’s hardly their fault.”

Cipher giggles. “You’re so mean sometimes. Did they teach you the art of the sneak diss at the nunnery?”

“I’m not a nun,” Hyacine says, a little miffed. “I’m a priestess. I’m meant to bring the blessings of the Titans to more people.”

“And you’re doing it,” Phainon says, giving her a winning smile. “Look at us! We’ve traveled across half of Amphoreus.”

It’s a pretty way of saying they’ve been on the run from the law for half a year. “Give me my winnings,” Mydei demands, holding out both hands. “I’m owed two tarts, last I checked.”

“Hey, you don’t get those until you win.”

Mydei shoves down the last shreds of his crumbling pride and looks up at Phainon through his lashes. “Please?”

Phainon’s hand twitches. He hands over both tarts.

Poor predictable Phainon, Mydei thinks, as he stuffs his face as fast as humanly possible. He’s just too easy.

Cipher taps her foot against the ground. “So what do we do now?”

“Just wait, I suppose,” Hyacine says. “They announce the winners in mid-afternoon. So… a little over an hour?”

Mydei starts on the second tart. This one has strawberries and cherries. Holy fuck. He’s changed his mind. Maybe this mafia town is alright if they make tarts this damn good.

All four of them head backstage to the competitors’ seating. Mydei isn’t entirely sure that the others are allowed to come with, but the backstage area has shade and the crowd doesn’t, so backstage it is. Hyacine gives them sandwiches she’d panic-packed that morning at the crack of dawn; Mydei and Phainon split their two sandwiches in half and share them. Cipher laughs and eats her tuna salad sandwich like someone’s going to take it from her.

And then, just as he finishes the second half of the sandwich, someone approaches Mydei and taps his shoulder.

“The judges want to speak to you.”

Mydei’s stomach turns. He gets up and follows them toward the stage, where the panel sits, deliberating.

There are five judges at the table. The woman in the center, the most battle-hardened, nods briskly as he approaches. “Young man,” she says. “Do you mind if we take a closer look at your armor?”

Mydei freezes. “You can’t take it off of me,” he says suddenly, before he can think better of it. “Don’t—don’t take it off.”

“Of course not,” the judge says. She stands up and examines the armor carefully, squinting at the engravings. “This is indeed an admirable replica of the Deliverer’s armor of legend. I’m impressed by your dedication.”

“…Thank you,” Mydei says, instead of telling her that it’s the real Deliverer’s armor, and that it isn’t his. “I respect him very much. The Deliverer, I mean. The stories of him.”

“I can tell,” says another one of the judges, beaming at him. “Not only is the armor an excellent design, but the jewelry suits the traditional wear of the Deliverer’s lover in legends. It’s a bold choice; most people would choose to imitate the legendary hero himself, but you’ve chosen to dress as a Deliverer’s lover instead. Very interesting.”

The sweetness of the tarts suddenly turns sour in his mouth. “I’m not the Deliverer’s—you know. I’m not—we’re not like that.”

“Right,” says the center judge, with a weathered smile. “Well, I think we’ve come to a decision. Please be ready backstage.”

Mydei’s heart leaps into his throat. That sounds like they’re going to be announcing him as a winner. But they announce the top five places. He could be any of those. The only prize he wants is the Coreflame, and that’s reserved for first place.

He steadies himself backstage, waiting for his number. Four hundred five, he chants to himself. Four hundred five. Four hundred five.

“—and the grand prize goes to number four hundred and five!”

Mydei blinks. What?

Someone beckons him forward. He stumbles out into the blinding afternoon light, still reeling. Even for all their effort, he didn’t think he’d actually win. And yet here he is, standing on the Tretos stage, shaking the hands of the judges in a blur.

Maybe this is the magic of the Deliverer’s quest, Mydei wonders, half-delirious. Maybe Phainon’s uncanny luck extends to him, too, just this once.

“This competitor showed incredible creativity and familiarity with the legends of the Deliverers, the heroes who once graced Amphoreus with their light in previous eons. From the armor to the jewelry to the incredibly coordinated duel, ending in a glorious loss at the hands of the legendary hero, every aspect of this performance embodied the ideals of the Grand Chrysos Competition—”

Mydei searches the crowd, trying to spot Phainon. He’s criminally easy to find, with that bright white hair. Also because he’s sitting on Cipher’s shoulders, cheering with all his might. What a dork. Mydei’s crush on him is pitiable.

“—will commence at sundown, with the first dance led by our victor and his wife!”

Mydei frowns. Led by him? And—

“Thank you all for coming, and please enjoy the festivities!”

As soon as the microphone is off, Mydei flags down the announcer. “A dance?” he asks, in a half-whisper. “And my wife? What is going on?”

“Ah, it’s a traditional thing! The first dance of the evening’s festivities is led by the victor of the competition. Celia—the innkeeper—told me you were here with your wife. She can naturally join you as well.”

“Mydei, you bastard, you really did it!!”

Mydei’s heart sinks. Yeah, that’s Cipher’s voice. And she’s definitely right behind him.

“This must be your wife, yes?”

Cipher blinks as she skids to a halt beside him. “Your…”

“Yes,” Mydei says through gritted teeth. “This is my wife, Cipher, who is a reputable citizen and has never done anything inadvisable.”

Cipher kicks his shin. Mydei tries to step on her foot, but misses, as always.

“We’ll see you two for the first dance of the night then, yes?”

“Of course,” Cipher says brightly, in what passes remarkably well as a polite voice. “We’d be delighted! And I’m so glad you appreciated the effort in Mydei’s performance. He’s worked really hard to look like the Deliverer’s lover, you know.”

“Cipher,” Mydei hisses under his breath. If only he could land a hit on her. Just once.

“See ya!” Cipher calls to the organizers, and whisks him away, so fast it’s almost magical.

***

“And we get free dinner,” Phainon says dreamily, piling up his plate even higher with more grilled fish. “This is my favorite mission ever. Why can’t every Coreflame mission be like this? I’ll take a chivalry competition over fighting a hundred Titankin any day. And then a free meal afterwards? This is paradise.”

Cipher rolls her eyes. “Every meal would be free if you let me work a little of my magic.”

“But this is so much better than theft,” Phainon says, beaming as he chows down on another piece of fish. “Hey, Mydei—don’t you want some more? It’s your feast, after all.”

Mydei feels sick to his stomach. He hasn’t told Phainon about the dance thing yet, and Cipher hasn’t either, apparently. “I’ve already had plenty.”

It isn’t that he hates Cipher or anything. She’s a great friend and companion, all things considered. But to make such a public proclamation, to dance with her and to tell thousands of people that they’re married, makes him feel nauseous. He’s terrified of Phainon’s reaction. He can’t decide which would be worse: blatant jealousy, or nothing at all. What Mydei wouldn’t give for Phainon to look at him with the soft wrath of jealousy in his eyes. To want him so publicly. To say, This is one of my belongings, and command his eternal loyalty.

“Stop looking at me like that,” Phainon says, with a nervous-sounding laugh. “Mydei, are you alright? You’ve been spacing out.”

“I’m fine,” Mydei says. Then, with a glance at the sky, “It’s almost sundown.”

Cipher nods. She stands from the table and stretches her spine. “Showtime, huh?”

Mydei steels his resolve and stands up with her.

“Oh, right! You still have to get the Coreflame.” Phainon frowns at them, confused. “But Cipher, why are you going along? I thought Mydei would receive the prize alone.”

“It’s nothing,” Mydei mutters, like a coward. “We’ll be back soon.”

And then he flees, tail between his legs.

Cipher whistles lowly as they retreat. “Damn. You know, I can’t decide which of you is more pathetic.”

Mydei just sighs through his nose. He can’t bring himself to argue. “Just shut up and get this over with.”

Mercifully, Cipher taps their shoulders together and then shuts her mouth.

“The grand prize, Tretos’ famed Coreflame, will be granted to our winner, number four hundred and five, Mydeimos!”

Mydei stands beside the organizers. They hand the Coreflame over to him. It’s warmer than he’d expected. Usually Phainon handles all the Coreflames they’ve collected, so Mydei never lays hands on them. But this one is his. He takes it and lets it sink into his hand, the half-tangible ball glowing as it touches him. Its warmth slowly spreads into his arm, his chest, his heart. It’s sort of beautiful, having a piece of the world contained within him. Is this how Phainon feels all the time, holding the whole world in his chest?

“And now, for the first dance of the evening, led by our victor and his wife!”

Cipher flashes him a smile that’s half a grimace. She holds out her hand.

With apprehension, Mydei takes it. “You lead.”

For once, Cipher doesn’t take advantage of his distress. She just steps in time with the music and leads him into a simple waltz.

It’s strange, watching Cipher move so slowly. Usually she’s a ball of energy, zooming around everywhere at once. But here, she moves deliberately, leading Mydei in a slow revolution, one hand on his shoulder to keep him grounded. It’s surprisingly easy to move alongside her. Maybe all that battle experience has made them more in sync with each other.

Either way, the dreaded dance ends quickly. Mydei bows to the crowd and then to Cipher, and heads back to their table feeling relieved.

“Pretty good, right?” Cipher says, preening, as she plunks herself back into her chair. “I didn’t step on your feet at all.”

“Yeah,” Mydei admits, giving her a rare hint of a smile. His appetite has returned with a vengeance, so he loads up his plate with more fish and potatoes and asparagus. “Not too bad.”

“Great work, you two,” Hyacine says, as she returns to the table with an entire tray of desserts. “Now let’s enjoy the night!”

Mydei digs into his dinner like he hasn’t eaten all day. The food goes above and beyond his expectations—it’s excellently seasoned, and the vegetables and fish are clearly fresh. The weather is still horrible, but at least the nighttime is cooler, and at least the Coreflame is stable in his chest. Maybe Tretos isn’t so bad, after all.

And then, halfway through his meal, he looks up across the table.

Phainon is stone-faced and silent.

Suddenly Mydei feels too hot again. That expression can’t bode well. “Deliverer. Tell me what’s wrong.”

Phainon’s mouth narrows. “Can I talk to you?”

Mydei takes another bite of his fish. “Uh huh.”

“Alone.”

Mydei nearly bites his tongue. “Okay,” he says. “Take me away, then.”

Phainon takes the expression literally; he grabs Mydei’s wrist and drags him out of the town square, down a side alleyway, and all the way to the water’s edge. His grip is harsh, almost bruising. They’re way further than a simple private conversation demands.

When he finally comes to a standstill, Mydei pulls his wrist back. The afterecho of his grip still stings. What’s gotten into him? He opens his mouth to say something, and then—

Phainon slams him against the wall and crushes their mouths together.

Mydei stands there, completely still, eyes wide open, as Phainon kisses him. It’s messy, harsh, and entirely one-sided. Mydei is going cross-eyed trying to keep his eyes on Phainon. He feels dizzy. Phainon gives him no escape, holding his face in both hands and drawing him close.

At long last Phainon breaks away. His breath is ragged. “Mydei,” he rasps. “Please, Mydei.”

“Please what?” Mydei says, like an idiot. He’s gasping for breath too, his eyes blown wide.

Phainon sighs out a long breath. He lets go of Mydei’s face and buries his face in his bare shoulder. “You must know by now,” he murmurs against his skin. “Surely you’ve seen the way I look at you.”

Mydei’s breath catches. “Yeah,” he breathes, instead of saying something reasonable. “Yeah. I know.”

Phainon raises his head. “Is that all you have to say?” he asks, so quietly that his voice nearly breaks. “Do you not wish to be something of mine?”

The words get stuck in his throat. Mydei tries to say something, but nothing seems like it’ll come out right.

Phainon sighs and drops his head back down. “Forgive me my selfishness. Just once more. Please.”

This time, when Phainon lifts his head again, Mydei lets his eyes slip closed. It feels like it takes ages for Phainon’s mouth to find his again, but when it does, it’s thrilling, like sparks brushing his skin. Phainon kisses him slow, open-mouthed but not very assertive. Mydei exhales in between kisses, when their mouths separate just slightly, and then he buries his hands in Phainon’s hair and kisses him back, hard and uncoordinated and a little delirious.

At long last Phainon wrests himself away. When Mydei pulls him closer again, he looks bewildered.

“Never again,” says Mydei, his voice rough. “Promise me you will never again even entertain the idea of saying I belong to someone else. I am your sword, your shield, your unswerving companion. Do not let yourself doubt it.”

Phainon’s eyes are wide and clear blue, dyed red and gold by the last lingering sun’s rays. The Coreflame in Mydei’s chest hums, like it’s happy to be in proximity of its other halves.

“For fuck’s sake,” Mydei grumbles, letting go of his hair. “If you’re just going to stand there staring at me then—”

Phainon drops to one knee.

Mydei looks down at him. “Really?” he asks, a little amused. “Are your legs so weak, Deliverer, that you collapse at the slightest provocation?”

Phainon laughs breathily. “Has no one ever sworn their loyalty to you before?”

Mydei blinks. The truth is that no one has. But when he looks down again, sees Phainon knelt before him without his armor, just him and his honor laid bare, it suddenly makes sense.

Something in his chest feels odd. “You don’t need to do this. I am your sword. I will fight beside you regardless.”

“But you aren’t,” Phainon says. “You aren’t my sword.” Here he draws himself to his feet again, standing up to his full height to look him in the eye. “Mydei, you are—you are the gems encrusted in the crown. You are the gleam on the sharp edge of my blade. You are the steadiness in my hands and the sureness in my steps. Of course I would want to keep you for myself.”

This time when he reaches out, only his fingertips brush against Mydei’s cheek, like he’s scared to touch him.

Mydei huffs a sigh. “Are you done?”

Phainon retracts his hand. He clears his throat, his face faintly red. “Yeah. I’m done.”

“Good,” Mydei says. Then he throws a punch directly at Phainon’s stomach.

Phainon wheezes as he takes the hit full-on. But his eyes sharpen, and then before Mydei’s second punch can connect, he’s already leaping out of the way, down towards the water.

Mydei keeps advancing, throwing punch after punch and kick after kick. Phainon dodges each one expertly, retreating backwards to stay just out of his reach. He laughs as Mydei misses yet again, retreating another step.

“Come on, Mydei,” he taunts, grinning ear to ear. “You can do better than that, can’t you?”

“Hm,” says Mydei. He takes one more step forward.

Phainon backs up that last, crucial step. Then he tumbles backwards into the water with a shriek.

Mydei watches, amused, as he surfaces, spluttering, from the water. “Hey!” he yells, shaking his hair off like a dog as he clambers back up to the pier. “That was—that was dirty!”

“Not my fault you weren’t looking behind you.”

Phainon chokes on a laugh as he coughs the water out. He’s soaked through, his wet clothes clinging to him like soggy paper. He looks pathetic. Mydei thinks he’s never liked him more.

“Well, come on,” Mydei says, offering him a hand. “Let’s go.”

Phainon’s laugh sparkles like the water beneath them. “That’s it?” he says, grinning as he shoves his sopping wet hair out of his face. “Don’t you want to tell me I’m the dumbest man to ever live and dramatically run away, leaving me destitute?”

“No,” Mydei says. “I never want to leave.”

Phainon’s eyes go wide.

“And you look like shit,” Mydei adds, just because he can. “Your hair is all flat. And your crown is falling off your head.”

Phainon looks at him. Mydei looks back. They stare at each other in silence.

He can’t be sure which of them laughs first. But before he knows it, Phainon is doubled over cackling, his wet hair flinging droplets onto Mydei’s clothes, and Mydei is struggling to breathe through the snickering.

When the laughter finally dies, they’re left standing in the dark, gasping for breath. It’s strangely intimate, this shared joy. Mydei doesn’t even know what it’s for. It doesn’t matter. It’s him and Phainon and they’re never going to be apart again.

“We’re good, right?” Phainon asks eventually, looking up at the dark sky.

Mydei looks over at him instead. “Yeah,” he says, smiling just a little. “Yeah, we’re good.”

Phainon smiles. He breathes out a sigh. He bumps their shoulders together. Then he starts walking back towards the town square, where the party is still raging.

Mydei falls into step beside him. He walks a little too close, enough that the warmth in his chest expands. “Do you want me to give you the Coreflame now?”

Phainon shrugs.

Mydei raises an eyebrow at him. “What kind of answer is that?”

“I don’t mind if you keep it.”

“But you’re the Deliverer. You’re supposed to carry all the Coreflames to keep them safe until we reach the Vortex of Genesis.”

“It’s safe with you,” Phainon says, looking over at him. “If you and I are to stay together, then it’s just as safe in your heart as it is in mine.”

“That’s the problem, Deliverer. What if I were to betray you? Where would you be then?”

“You won’t,” says Phainon simply, and then he says no more.

They round the corner back towards the town square. The music is more upbeat now, an energetic group dance instead of the slow tune of before. The town has lit fires to illuminate everyone. The desserts are piled high. “Yeah,” Mydei whispers. “I won’t.”

Phainon looks over at him. He opens his mouth.

“There you are!” Hyacine calls, running over. “Mydei, they brought out strawberry cake, so I saved you two slices! And you never finished your juice, so—”

“They made me dance four more times,” Cipher whines from their left, appearing out of nowhere. “You guys are so mean to me. I had to run away in between songs so they wouldn’t keep forcing me up there.”

“Sucks to be you, I guess,” Mydei says, slapping her on the back. It actually connects this time. Cipher yelps at the touch, her hair bristling like fur.

“Be nice,” Hyacine demands, shoving the cake into Mydei’s hands. “And besides, I don’t think the dancing was too terrible. I was an alright partner, wasn't I?”

“Better than him,” Cipher drawls, kicking Mydei in the shin. “Hey, hero boy, what happened to you? You’re soaked.”

“Ah, nothing much,” Phainon says, beaming. “Just the usual.”

“I won,” says Mydei, crossing his arms and letting himself gloat for a moment.

Phainon rolls his eyes. “You cheated. I ought to demand a rematch.”

“And get your ass handed to you again?”

“Not fighting, Mydei.” Phainon takes his hand and pulls him toward the town square’s center. “Dancing.”

His hand is firm and steady. You are the steadiness in my hands, Mydei thinks, and smiles to himself. Nothing much, indeed. Nothing much at all.

Part of him wonders what Phainon was about to say, before the rest of their party found them. What he would have said if they were alone for that one extra moment. But Mydei thinks he already knows, because Phainon has said it to him a thousand times without ever shaping the words.

He could ask, he knows. He could ask Phainon right now, and he’d say it.

But Mydei doesn’t need to ask. This is enough, he thinks. Even if Phainon never finds the words for it, this is enough.

“You’re on, Deliverer,” he says, letting his smile widen.

Phainon leads him into the town square. Together, they dance.
